title: Repetitive Questions in Dementia: How Caregivers Should Respond Without Arguing
description: Why does someone living with dementia ask the same question again and again? Repetitive questioning can be one of the most exhausting parts of dementia caregiving. You may answer the question clearly, only to hear it again a few minutes—or even a few seconds—later. This educational explainer breaks down why repetitive questions happen and gives caregivers a practical, respectful way to respond without arguing, shaming, testing the person’s memory, or repeatedly offering long explanations. In this video, you will learn: • Why repetitive questioning happens in dementia • Why the person may not retain the question or your answer • How anxiety, confusion, pain, hunger, thirst, fatigue, constipation, noise, and changes in routine may contribute • Why repetitive questioning is usually not intentional manipulation • How to respond with one brief, truthful answer • How to acknowledge the emotion behind the question • When written notes, clocks, and visual reminders may help • How to redirect gently toward a safe and pleasant activity • What caregivers should avoid saying • Why sudden or rapidly fluctuating changes require medical attention • Stroke warning signs that require an immediate 911 call • Why medication is not a routine solution for repetitive questioning A useful response sequence is: 1. Pause and approach calmly. 2. Check for immediate safety concerns. 3. Give one short and truthful answer. 4. Acknowledge the likely emotion. 5. Consider possible contributors such as discomfort, pain, hunger, fatigue, anxiety, or sensory overload. 6. Try one practical support if it does not increase confusion. 7. Redirect gently toward something safe and familiar. Instead of saying: “I already told you.” Try: “Lunch is at noon. I’ll remind you when it gets closer.” Or, when the person appears anxious: “You are safe with me right now.” The goal is not to test their memory or force them to remember. The goal is to reduce distress, preserve dignity, and respond to what the person may be experiencing in that moment. A sudden change in behavior, alertness, speech, walking, vision, strength, or balance should not automatically be blamed on dementia. Seek prompt professional guidance for sudden or rapidly fluctuating changes. Call 911 immediately for possible stroke symptoms such as facial drooping, one-sided weakness or numbness, new speech difficulty, sudden vision or walking problems, loss of balance, or a sudden severe headache. In this video, I walk caregivers through a dementia home safety assessment. Because when someone you love is living with dementia, the home can change. The front door can become a wandering risk. The back door can become a safety concern. The kitchen can become dangerous. The bathroom can become a fall risk. Medication left out on the counter can become a serious problem. And the same house that once felt familiar can become confusing, overwhelming, or unsafe depending on the stage of dementia. This is why home safety is not just about “baby-proofing” a house. It is about understanding dementia, understanding risk, and thinking one step ahead. In this video, we talk about: * Dementia home safety * Wandering prevention * Exit doors, front doors, back doors, garages, and side doors * Pool safety for people living with dementia * Why dementia stage matters * Mild, moderate, and severe dementia safety differences * Door locks, latches, and deadbolts * Interior bathroom and bedroom locks * Lighting changes and fall risk * Kitchen safety * Stove shutoffs and knob covers * When cooking may become unsafe * Protecting independence when possible * Removing kitchen hazards * Medications on counters * Sharp objects and toxic cleaners * Bathroom safety * Grab bars, non-slip mats, and toilet safety * Water temperature safety * Medication storage * Why caregivers need a home safety plan One of the biggest mistakes families make is waiting until something happens. A fall. A wandering episode. A stove left on. A medication mistake. A bathroom accident. A door locked from the inside. A person walking outside and not knowing how to get back. The goal is to begin with the end in mind. Look at the home through the eyes of the person living with dementia. Ask yourself: Can they leave the home without anyone knowing? Can they lock themselves in a room? Can they access knives, cleaners, medications, or appliances? Can they safely use the bathroom at night? Can they move from room to room without shadows, poor lighting, or trip hazards? Can they still cook safely, or does the kitchen need another layer of protection? There is no one rule that applies to every person. A person with mild dementia may still be able to cook, make decisions, and move through the home with check-ins and support. A person with moderate or severe dementia may need a very different safety plan. That is why staging the dementia matters. title: Dementia vs. Alzheimer’s: Dr. James Galvin Explains the Difference

In Part 2 of my conversation with Dr. James Galvin, we answer one of the most common questions families ask: Is dementia the same thing as Alzheimer’s disease? Dr. Galvin explains that dementia is a general term. It describes a change in memory or other thinking abilities that interferes with everyday activities. Alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause of dementia, but it is not the only cause. There are many different causes of dementia. Some are genetic. Some are not. Some may be reversible. Some progress quickly. Some progress slowly. That is why it matters to know what type of dementia someone may have. A diagnosis should not stop at “dementia.” Families should be asking: What is causing the dementia? Because the cause can affect the symptoms, the treatment path, the questions families should ask, and the type of support needed. Dr. Galvin uses a simple car example. A Ford, Mercedes, Toyota, and Tesla are all cars, but they are not the same car. They work differently. They require different repairs. The same idea applies to dementia. Dementia describes the problem. The cause helps guide the next step. title: Early Alzheimer’s Detection: Why Memory Screening Matters More Than Ever
description: Why does early Alzheimer’s and dementia detection matter more today than it did in the past? In this video, Dr. Erik explains why the conversation around Alzheimer’s disease is changing. For many years, dementia care was focused mostly on symptom management after the disease had already progressed. Families often waited until memory loss, behavior changes, confusion, or safety concerns became too obvious to ignore. But Alzheimer’s disease can begin many years before the first obvious symptoms appear. That means waiting until a crisis may leave families with fewer options, less time to plan, and more stress when decisions become urgent. title: Dementia After Hospitalization: 5 Questions Caregivers Must Ask Before Going Home
description: If your loved one is living with dementia and recently went to the hospital, please do not assume that discharge means everything will go back to baseline right away. Many caregivers tell me the same thing: “My loved one went into the hospital, and when they came home, everything was different.” They may be weaker. They may be more confused. They may refuse care. They may not sleep. They may be more anxious, more agitated, or less able to do the things they were doing before. That does not always mean the dementia suddenly got worse. After a hospital stay, a person living with dementia may go through a high-risk transition period because of delirium, sleep disruption, unfamiliar surroundings, medication changes, immobility, weakness, infection, pain, new incontinence, and loss of routine. The hospital may fix the immediate medical problem, but that does not always mean the person is functionally ready to return home without support. That is why caregivers need to ask better questions before discharge. In this video, I explain why dementia care can get harder after a hospital stay, what caregivers should watch for, and the five post-hospital questions I want every family to ask: 1. Are they back to baseline? 2. Could this be delirium? 3. What medications changed? 4. What physical function was lost? 5. What support does the caregiver need? These questions matter because the transition home is often where families feel unsupported, overwhelmed, and unsure what to do next. title: Grandparent Scams, AI Voice Cloning, and Dementia: How Families Can Stay Safe
description: If you are caring for someone living with dementia, scams are not just annoying phone calls anymore. They are becoming more personal, more believable, and more dangerous. With AI voice cloning, caller ID spoofing, deepfake video, and social engineering, families can no longer rely only on what they hear, what they see, or what appears on a phone screen. In this video, I talk about what dementia caregivers need to know about modern scams targeting older adults. I also share one simple protection strategy every family should consider: a private family password. Years ago, if your son called and sounded like your son, you believed it was your son. If caller ID showed your bank, Medicare, or a doctor’s office, many people trusted it. But today, scammers can clone voices, fake phone numbers, collect personal information online, and create emergencies that feel real. They may call a parent or grandparent and say there was an accident, they need money right away, or they are in danger. They may tell the person not to call anyone else. That urgency is part of the scam. This becomes even more concerning when the person receiving the call is older, isolated, overwhelmed, or living with dementia. That is why families need a plan before the phone rings. A family password can help. If someone calls asking for money, claiming there is an emergency, or pretending to be a loved one, ask for the password. If they cannot give it, hang up and call the person back using a number you already trust. I also talk about Medicare scams, fake genetic testing calls, identity theft, debit card risk, and why caregivers should be careful before giving personal information over the phone. title: Why Routine Matters in Dementia Care: 5 Daily Anchors for Caregivers
description: If your loved one is living with dementia and the day often feels chaotic, unpredictable, or emotionally exhausting, you are not failing. One of the most powerful tools caregivers can use is routine. But I want to be clear: routine does not mean controlling the person. Routine does not mean becoming rigid, forceful, or demanding. In dementia care, routine is about reducing the number of surprises the brain has to process. When someone is living with Alzheimer’s disease or another form of dementia, their brain may have a harder time processing changes, noise, choices, demands, and unfamiliar situations. That sensory overload can show up as confusion, anxiety, agitation, resistance, or emotional distress. In this video, I explain why routine can be reassuring in dementia care and how caregivers can build a daily rhythm around five important anchors: 1. Morning orientation 2. Meals and hydration 3. Hygiene and personal care 4. Meaningful activity 5. Evening wind down The goal is not to force your loved one into a strict schedule. The goal is to create a rhythm that helps them feel safer, more oriented, and less overwhelmed throughout the day. I also explain the difference between a schedule and a rhythm. A schedule is often driven by the caregiver’s agenda and can become rigid. A rhythm is more flexible. It uses familiar events, gentle cues, and repeated patterns to reduce confusion and help the person living with dementia understand what is happening next. title: Sudden Confusion in Dementia? Check for a UTI Before Blaming Dementia
description: If your loved one is living with dementia and suddenly seems much more confused, agitated, paranoid, weak, sleepy, or “not like themselves,” do not automatically assume the dementia is just getting worse. A sudden change in mental status can be a medical red flag. In this video, I explain why dementia usually progresses gradually, while sudden confusion over hours or days may point to delirium, infection, dehydration, pain, constipation, medication changes, abnormal labs, hospitalization, poor sleep, or another medical trigger. And one of the biggest things caregivers need to know is this: In older adults living with dementia, a UTI may not look like the classic UTI symptoms you expect. They may not say, “It burns when I urinate.” They may not have a clear fever. They may not be able to explain what hurts. Instead, the body may communicate through behavior. New agitation. Sudden confusion. Restlessness. Paranoia. Extreme sleepiness. New falls. Trouble walking. Loss of appetite. Withdrawal. That is why I always say: behavior is communication. title: When Healthcare Professionals Let Ego Get in the Way of Patient Care
description: This morning, I got a call from one of our nurse practitioners on my way to the office. Learn more here: medbetterhealth.org/guide She had been speaking with a physician about a patient and family situation. The stakes were high. There was a difference of opinion. Emotions were involved. That is what we call a crucial conversation. But instead of starting with curiosity, respect, and the shared goal of helping the patient and caregiver, the conversation started with an attack: “Are you even a real doctor?” Let’s pause there. Because when two healthcare professionals are speaking about a patient, the goal should not be ego. The goal should not be status. The goal should not be proving who is more important. The goal should be the patient. The caregiver. The family. When we attack someone personally, we shift the conversation away from the issue that matters. Instead of talking about what is best for the patient, we put the other person in defense mode. And once that happens, the collective knowledge in the room starts to shut down. In this video, I talk about why crucial conversations matter in healthcare, dementia care, caregiving, and leadership. A crucial conversation usually has three things: High stakes. Different opinions. Strong emotions. And if we do not recognize that moment, we can easily let ego, frustration, or tone take over. This matters for clinicians. It matters for nurse practitioners. It matters for physicians. It matters for administrators. And it matters for caregivers too. Because families caring for someone living with dementia also have crucial conversations every day. Can I keep doing this? Do we need more help? Is my loved one safe at home? Am I burning out? Do we need to talk about assisted living, respite, or other support? Those conversations are hard. title: Dementia Caregiver Burnout: Why You Still Need Respite
description: Have you ever tried to get respite as a dementia caregiver, only to get called back almost immediately? Maybe you finally arranged help. Maybe a home health aide or direct care worker came into the home. Maybe you thought, “Okay, I can finally step out for a few hours.” And then your loved one became agitated, anxious, aggressive, scared, or refused to let anyone else help. I want you to know something: That does not mean respite cannot work. It may mean the person coming into the home was not the right fit, was not trained in dementia care, or did not know how to approach someone living with dementia. In this video, I talk about a real conversation I had with a caregiver who told me she felt like she was “in jail” because every time she tried to leave, her mom could not tolerate anyone else being there. And I understand that feeling. You love your mom. You love your dad. You love your spouse. You love your grandma. But you cannot be the only person there 24/7. That is not healthy for you, and eventually, it is not healthy for them either. In dementia care, respite is not just about “getting someone to sit there.” The person coming in needs to understand dementia. They need to know how to smile, approach calmly, use the right tone, avoid creating fear, use familiar music, point to pictures, build trust, and step into the home in a way that does not make the person living with dementia feel threatened. Because if the person living with dementia feels unsafe, confused, rushed, or afraid, of course the caregiver may get called back. That does not mean you failed. It means the plan needs to be better. And caregivers, I want you to remember the airplane example: When the oxygen mask drops, you put your mask on first. Not because you do not love the person next to you. But because if you cannot breathe, you cannot help them. The same thing is true in dementia caregiving. If you do not take care of yourself, eventually you will not be able to keep taking care of your loved one. title: Before Antipsychotics for Dementia Behaviors, Watch This
description: Is your loved one living with dementia taking an antipsychotic medication for agitation, aggression, paranoia, or other behavioral symptoms? Before families think only about medication, caregivers need to understand the bigger picture. In dementia care, behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia — also called BPSD — can include agitation, aggression, paranoia, anxiety, hallucinations, and other behavior changes. And when those behaviors become overwhelming, the first instinct is often: “Can we give Mom something to calm her down?” But medications are not simple. Antipsychotic medications used in older adults with dementia-related psychosis can carry serious safety concerns, including a black box warning related to increased mortality risk. That does not mean medication is never used. It means these decisions need careful, ongoing clinician judgment. In this video, I explain why caregivers should talk with their loved one’s doctor, look for possible triggers, and ask whether non-medication interventions can be tried before relying only on medication for behavior control. Sometimes agitation is not random. It may be connected to the environment, clothing, noise, fear, confusion, feeling unsafe, thinking they are in the hospital, or believing someone moved or stole their belongings. Before jumping straight to medication, caregivers should ask: What changed? What happened right before the behavior? Could something in the environment be triggering fear? Could the person feel rushed, confused, unsafe, or misunderstood? Are there medical issues, pain, infection, dehydration, constipation, sleep problems, or medication changes involved? title: Dementia Accusations: Why They Happen and What Caregivers Should Do
description: Has your loved one living with dementia ever accused you of stealing their money? Or accused you of lying, abandoning them, or doing something that is not true? That can feel painful, embarrassing, and overwhelming for caregivers. But in many cases, these accusations are not really about the wallet, the money, or the object that went missing. They are often a fear signal. In this video, I explain dementia paranoia, why it can happen, and how caregivers can respond without escalating the situation. Paranoia, hallucinations, agitation, anxiety, sleep problems, appetite changes, apathy, and other behavior changes can fall under BPSD, which means behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia. When a person living with dementia accuses you of stealing, the instinct is usually to defend yourself. “I didn’t take it.” “You’re wrong.” “That never happened.” But arguing facts often makes the situation worse. Instead, the goal is to pause, validate the emotion, partner with your loved one, and redirect them toward something calmer and safer. If there is a sudden change in paranoia, confusion, agitation, or behavior, do not automatically blame dementia. Sudden changes can sometimes be connected to things like infection, pain, dehydration, constipation, medication changes, or lack of sleep. Speak with a healthcare professional if there is a sudden change in mental status or behavior. title: Mild, Moderate, and Severe Dementia: How to Know What Stage Your Loved One Is In
description: Learn more here: medbetterhealth.org/guide If your loved one has dementia, one of the most important questions you can ask is: What stage of dementia are they in? Because “dementia” by itself does not tell the caregiver what to do next. Mild dementia, moderate dementia, and severe dementia each come with different symptoms, risks, and caregiver responsibilities. In this video, I explain the difference between mild, moderate, and severe dementia, why dementia staging matters, and how tools like the FAST scale and Clinical Dementia Rating Scale can help professionals understand where someone is in the disease process. If you are caring for someone living with dementia in New York or Florida, MedBetterHealth may be able to support you through the GUIDE Model. The GUIDE Model is designed to help eligible families with dementia care education, caregiver support, care coordination, access to 24/7 support, and respite support when eligible. In early-stage dementia, the focus is planning. This may include legal planning, financial planning, medication safety, driving safety, home safety, family conversations, and building a support system while your loved one may still be able to participate in important decisions. In moderate dementia, the focus often shifts to safety, structure, supervision, and caregiver support. This is when families may start seeing more confusion, bathing and dressing challenges, wandering risk, sleep disruption, agitation, paranoia, hallucinations, repetitive questions, and increased caregiver stress. In severe dementia, the focus often becomes comfort, dignity, physical care, and goals of care. This may include skin care, oral care, swallowing concerns, aspiration risk, infection risk, pressure injury prevention, mobility support, hospice conversations, and full physical dependence. The stage of dementia changes the action plan. In the early stage, you plan. In the middle stage, you protect. In the late stage, you prioritize comfort and dignity. title: When Someone With Dementia Refuses Medication: What Caregivers Should Do
description: Start here to learn about GUIDE Model support: https://medbetterhealth.org/guide Has your loved one with dementia ever refused to take their medication? You come in and say, “Mom, you have to take these meds.” And she says, “No. I’m not taking that.” If this is happening in your home, you are not alone. In this episode of Straight Talk with Dr. Erik, I talk about why medication refusal happens in dementia and why caregivers should not assume it is “just behavior.” Sometimes there is a physical reason. Maybe the person has trouble swallowing. Maybe the medication causes nausea, dizziness, stomach discomfort, or another side effect. Sometimes there is a cognitive reason. The person may not believe they are sick or may not understand why the medication is needed. Sometimes there is a psychological reason. Paranoia, fear, distrust, or confusion can make a person believe the medication is harmful. And sometimes the issue is environmental. A rushed caregiver, a noisy room, a change in routine, or a new person giving the medication can all make refusal worse. In this video, I walk through practical caregiver strategies, including: • finding out why the refusal is happening • speaking with the doctor about side effects • asking whether a medication is still necessary • making medication time part of a calm routine • using simple language instead of arguing • avoiding medication “battles” • asking about alternate forms like patches, liquids, or sprinkles when appropriate • involving the pharmacist and medical team • tracking patterns around refusal This is not about forcing someone. It is about understanding what the behavior may be communicating and working with the right medical professionals to make the process safer and calmer. title: Don’t Argue With Dementia Reality
description: You know what I always tell caregivers? Do not argue with dementia reality. Because in your mind, you are telling the truth. But in their mind, you may be taking away the only reality they understand in that moment. My grandmother once asked, “Where is my mother?” Now logically, the answer was simple. Her mother had passed away. So my mom said the truth. She said, “Your mother passed away.” And what happened? My grandmother became angry. She felt hurt. She felt betrayed. She thought my mom was lying to her. And my mom is the caregiver. She is the one showing up every day. She is the one caring for her. So imagine how painful that is. This is why I tell families: Sometimes logic is not the right tool. With dementia, you have to meet the person where they are emotionally. So instead of arguing, I validated. I said, “Yes, Grandma, your mother went to the store.” Then I redirected her. We looked at pictures. We talked about family. And the whole situation calmed down. That is the lesson. You are not trying to win the argument. You are trying to lower the distress. You are trying to protect the person. You are trying to protect the caregiver. Validation first. Redirection second. Because if someone living with dementia sees the world through different glasses, you cannot force them to see through yours. title: Why Dementia Behaviors Are Not Random
description: You know what I always tell caregivers? Behavior is not random. When someone living with dementia starts yelling, accusing, pacing, resisting care, or acting completely different, we cannot just say, “That’s dementia.” We have to ask, “What happened before the behavior?” Because many times, there is a trigger. Maybe they are seeing something differently. Maybe they are hearing something differently. Maybe they are in pain and cannot explain it. Maybe they are dehydrated. Maybe they have an infection. Maybe a medication was changed. Maybe they just came home from the hospital with a whole new list of pills and nobody explained what changed. So we have to slow down. There is something called the ABC model. Antecedent. Behavior. Consequence. In simple language: What happened before? What did they do? What happened after? Because if their reality is altered, their emotions change. And when their emotions change, their behavior follows. So instead of asking, “Why are they acting like this?” Ask, “What are they reacting to?” That one question changes everything. And caregivers, please remember this: If your loved one suddenly changes, advocate. Ask about infection. Ask about dehydration. Ask about pain. Ask about medications. Ask what changed after the hospital. Because if you do not advocate, many things can get missed. title: Why Dementia Gets Worse Later in the Day
description: You know what I always tell caregivers about sundowning? It usually does not come out of nowhere. A lot of families will say, “Dr. Erik, every day around 3, 4, 5 o’clock, Mom starts getting confused. She gets agitated. She gets restless. She is not herself.” And yes, that can happen with dementia. But we have to ask why. Because by that time of day, the person may already be tired. Their brain has been working all day. They may have had too much noise, too much TV, too many people talking, too much stimulation. Then the lighting starts changing. The shadows start coming in. The room feels different. And for someone living with dementia, that can become confusing very quickly. So what do we do? We create routine. Not a loose routine. A real routine. Same bedtime. Same wake-up time. Morning light coming in. Curtains closed at night so shadows are not moving around the room. Motion-sensor lights if they need to get up to use the bathroom. Less noise later in the day. No loud movies. No blasting music. No heavy dinner, caffeine, or too much fluid right before bed. Because little things matter. A shadow matters. A loud room matters. A late cup of tea matters. A change in routine matters. And sometimes those little things are what sink the whole ship. So if your loved one is sundowning, don’t only ask, “How do I stop the behavior?” Ask, “What is happening in the environment before the behavior starts?” That question changes everything. title: If Dementia Hallucinations Suddenly Start, Do This First
description: You know what I always tell caregivers? If mom has had dementia for a while, and she has been seeing things or hearing things for months, that is one situation. But if everything was okay yesterday… And now today, she is suddenly seeing people, seeing strings, hearing voices, acting strange, or saying things that are completely new? Do not just say, “Oh, that’s the dementia.” That is where you have to slow down. Because sometimes, when a person living with dementia suddenly changes, there may be something else going on. It could be an infection. It could be a medication issue. It could be dehydration. It could be sodium. It could be something medical that needs to be checked. And one of the first things I think about is a UTI. Now, sometimes you go to the doctor and they say, “No, no, this is dementia.” But if this is new, you have to advocate. You can say, “Doctor, I understand. But this is a sudden change. Can we at least check a urinalysis and basic labs?” Because the lesson is this: When something is new, look into it. Better safe than sorry. Dementia can cause hallucinations, yes. But sudden changes should not be brushed off. Caregivers know their loved one better than anybody. If something feels off, speak up.
